First of all, the folks in here are right to be paranoid, given Google's proclivities towards data gathering, and recent tendencies of important software to contain blatant spyware as a "feature."

Second I will warn you I have never tried to do packet analysis on Android traffic, nor have I made any attempt to examine Android public source code, or the binaries.

However, my personal belief is that no, Android does not track you.

And therein lies the rub. Android. Vanilla Android that almost nobody uses except for testing purposes of one sort or another, that has its source code completely open and available to everyone without hassle. The type that just about no phone or tablet maker will install on their devices out of the factory, and that you'd have to put on yourself, probably manually. IIRC those phone manufacturers also have to release their code for some portions of the OS (depending on the OSS license, e.g. they would have to release any changes to the kernel), but good luck auditing 50 variants of the same operating system. Plus there are a lot of components that a phone manufacturer provides that are NOT going to be covered by these licenses.

Vanilla Android doesn't have a lot of things, including Chrome and (IIRC) Play, and just about anything else. If you want a "Vanilla Android" experience, download the Android devkit and run the emulator. "Sparse" doesn't quite cover it; it's functional enough that you could probably set up the software you need, but it would be tedious at best. Vanilla Windows installs come with more software. It also doesn't have any specialized tweaks, and probably no specialized drivers, if they're needed for some specific gadgets on the phone, so its utility is somewhat lacking from the get-go.

That said, a very large portion of web tracking occurs with things such as cookies, and those aren't OS-specific. You're just as vulnerable no matter what browser/OS/hardware combination you have, although in some cases a browser may or may not lack support for the particular trick that tracking group uses (hey, you could theoretically be using Lynx from 1999, after all), and you can put an ad blocker of one sort or another into use.

Additionally, as stated, OEMs like to put a lot of apps on there. Some are due to a deal, some are purchased by the OEM for you, some are made by the OEM for you. And each one might or might not track you, and each might or might not do so to varying degrees. Given the proliferation of the web in terms of apps, it's become pretty easy to slap on some usage data analyzer that occasionally throws a pack of information back to the app maker. Whether or not they're open about it and whether or not that's acceptable, that depends on the specific situation, and I can't really comment on it.

Plus it's always possible Google slipped something into Chrome. People have been suspicious of it for years; that's one reason why some people run straight Chromium (which is, truth be told, also pretty good, but good luck finding a designated "stable" version).

So, the answer is that there is no short answer, but for practical purposes, both on desktop and mobile, you can be tracked and probably will be tracked. Desktop has more provisions for dodging this. On mobile, some pre-installed apps may also be more prone to this, especially since some of them are a lot more necessary (once again, Google Play, for instance).
